output.impression: Multi-domain cognitive impairment with amnestic predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline. Episodic memory is profoundly impaired (RAVLT immediate recall 3rd percentile, delayed recall below the 1st percentile) and recognition does not compensate (1st percentile), consistent with a storage-type deficit. Semantic fluency (Animals, 8th percentile) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 18th percentile) are impaired; letter fluency (FAS, 22nd percentile), set-shifting (Trail Making B, 12th percentile) and figure copy (20th percentile) are reduced. Processing speed (Trail Making A, 25th percentile) is at the lower limit of normal. Mood screen borderline (GDS 5/15); the cognitive deficits are disproportionate to it. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 16/30.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O. Acellular CSF (WBC 2 cells/uL, no red cells) with normal protein (43.3 mg/dL) and glucose (64.6 mg/dL, CSF/serum ratio 0.57). Decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/40 ratio (0.042) with elevated p-tau181 (88 pg/mL) and total tau (545 pg/mL): amyloid-positive, p-tau-positive biomarker profile of Alzheimer-type pathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 21/30 with delayed recall 0/3 not improved by phonemic cues, informant-confirmed decline over two years, and loss of instrumental independence (finances taken over, no longer drives alone after getting lost), placing the syndrome at the dementia stage
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history and functional staging
action_criteria.rationale: Two years of decline reported by her wife must be measured on a validated instrument and staged by whether instrumental independence is lost before it can be attributed [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic profile with profoundly impaired delayed recall and recognition, plus impaired semantic fluency and naming, with a borderline mood screen that does not account for the deficits
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing defines the amnestic multi-domain profile beyond the bedside screen and sets a baseline for tracking [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal TSH, folate, RPR, HIV, electrolytes, hepatic function and inflammatory markers; B12 260 pg/mL in the low-normal range on long-term metformin; HbA1c 7.2% as a vascular risk factor to manage
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, syphilis, HIV and metabolic derangement are treatable contributors and must be screened before the decline is attributed to a neurodegenerative cause [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylmalonic acid within the reference range (0.31 umol/L), so the low-normal vitamin level does not reflect tissue deficiency
action_criteria.label: Measure methylmalonic acid to interpret the low-normal vitamin B12
action_criteria.rationale: A serum B12 of 260 pg/mL after 12 years of metformin, with reduced vibration sense at the toes, is indeterminate; methylmalonic acid shows whether functional deficiency contributes [BSH_B12_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral medial temporal atrophy (MTA 3) with temporoparietal volume loss disproportionate to age, plus moderate small vessel disease (Fazekas 2, two left putaminal lacunes) as a vascular contribution
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with the dementia (volumetric) protocol
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows the pattern of atrophy and the extent of cerebrovascular disease in a woman with diabetes, hypertension and a smoking history, and excludes hydrocephalus and mass lesions [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No contraindicating interaction; aspirin adds gastrointestinal risk and weight loss may affect glycemic control, both to counsel on
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against the current medicines before starting a cholinesterase inhibitor
action_criteria.rationale: Before a cholinesterase inhibitor is started, her aspirin and metformin should be reviewed for gastrointestinal and weight effects; neither changes the choice, so the check is optional [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the decline to depression or normal aging: the deficits are disproportionate to a GDS of 5/15 and she has lost instrumental independence
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Address safety: after getting lost on a familiar route she should not drive until a formal driving evaluation; keep finances with her wife, arrange supervision of medicines and plan caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, counseling on gastrointestinal symptoms with aspirin and on weight loss [NICE_NG97]
Treat the vascular contribution: continue blood pressure, statin and glycemic management with lacunes and moderate white matter disease on MRI, and support regular exercise
Reassess mood (GDS 5/15, social withdrawal) and treat depression if confirmed

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET]

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the dementia work-up; her pulse is regular at 79 and she has no syncope, palpitations or conduction history
Echocardiography does not contribute; the lacunes are small-vessel lesions, not embolic infarcts, and there is no murmur or heart failure
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; there is no syncope, palpitations or embolic-pattern infarct
Head CT adds nothing when MRI is available and tolerated; MRI is the structural study for the dementia work-up

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment (as a contributor, mixed dementia)
differential.key_features: Diabetes, hypertension, former smoking, Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease and two putaminal lacunes contribute; but the course is gradual, there is no stroke history, and memory-led decline with MTA grade 3 points to Alzheimer disease as the primary cause
No fluctuations, visual hallucinations (confirmed by her wife), REM sleep behavior disorder or parkinsonism
No personality or behavioral change beyond withdrawal; naming difficulty without aphasia; temporoparietal and medial temporal rather than frontal atrophy
Social withdrawal and borderline GDS 5/15, but recall is not rescued by cues or recognition and the deficits are disproportionate to mood; depression may coexist

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or infectious cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Normal TSH, folate, RPR, HIV, electrolytes and hepatic function; B12 260 pg/mL with normal methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; diabetes controlled (HbA1c 7.2%)

key_clinical_evidence: Insidious, progressive amnestic decline with impairment in additional domains and loss of instrumental independence meets the NIA-AA 2011 clinical criteria for probable Alzheimer disease dementia; medial temporal atrophy on MRI supports the diagnosis [NIA_AA_2011]
Delayed recall that neither cueing nor recognition rescues indicates a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit, the typical cognitive signature of Alzheimer disease
A low-normal B12 in a long-term metformin user is indeterminate; methylmalonic acid decides whether it contributes [BSH_B12_2014]
Cholinesterase inhibitors are the first-line symptomatic treatment for mild to moderate Alzheimer dementia; memantine is for moderate or severe disease [NICE_NG97]

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI showing medial temporal atrophy with moderate small vessel disease. Recommended: methylmalonic acid for the low-normal B12. Optional: amyloid status by CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET (one conclusive test), and a donepezil interaction check.
key_educational_points: Early AD classically presents with progressive episodic memory loss as the predominant symptom
Reversible causes of dementia must be systematically excluded with appropriate laboratory testing
Comorbid vascular disease is common in elderly AD patients and may contribute to cognitive decline (mixed dementia)
APOE genotype is a risk modifier and is not a diagnostic test for Alzheimer disease
Hippocampal atrophy on MRI is a supportive but not pathognomonic finding for AD
CSF biomarkers (Abeta42/40, phospho-tau, total tau) or amyloid PET establish Alzheimer pathology in vivo; one conclusive test is enough
Cholinesterase inhibitors remain first-line pharmacotherapy for mild-to-moderate AD
Driving safety must be addressed when patients demonstrate navigational impairment

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Sharma is a 69-year-old right-handed retired hospital pharmacy technician who is brought to the outpatient neurology clinic by her wife, Dorothy, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties. Dorothy reports that she first noticed something was wrong approximately two years ago when her wife began misplacing her car keys and wallet repeatedly, something she had never done before. She initially attributed it to normal aging, but over the past eight months the problems have become much more apparent and concerning. She now frequently asks the same questions multiple times within a single conversation, sometimes within minutes, and does not seem to recall that she already asked. She has forgotten several scheduled appointments with her primary care physician and her barber despite having kept these routines reliably for decades. Last Thanksgiving, she could not remember the name of her grandson's wife, whom she has known for six years, causing considerable embarrassment and family concern. Her daughter reports that when she calls to tell her about upcoming family plans, she has no recollection of the conversation the following day. She was previously an avid reader of history books but has stopped reading in the past year because she says she cannot remember what happened in previous chapters. She attempted to help her wife with preparing their tax documents this past winter, a task she had always managed independently, but became confused by the forms and gave up after making several errors. Her wife has since taken over managing their finances. She has also had difficulty operating the new television remote control and the microwave, despite being shown how to use them on multiple occasions. She got lost driving home from the hardware store two months ago, a route she has taken hundreds of times over thirty years, and had to call her wife for directions. Since then, the family has asked her not to drive alone. She continues to dress and bathe independently, though her wife notes she has worn the same outfit two days in a row on several occasions without realizing it. She denies any hallucinations, and her wife confirms there have been no episodes of seeing things that are not there. There have been no significant personality or behavioral changes, though she has become somewhat more withdrawn and less interested in socializing with friends from her lodge. She denies headaches, seizures, falls, tremor, or difficulty walking. Her sleep has been unremarkable with no acting out of dreams reported by her wife.

neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp or palmomental reflexes. No snout reflex. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements full bilaterally without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial sensation intact. Face symmetric with normal strength. Hearing mildly diminished bilaterally, age-appropriate. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady with normal base and stride. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative. No festination, no shuffling.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; knows month and year but states the date as three days prior and gives the wrong day of the week. MMSE 21/30, losing points on recall (0/3 at 5 minutes), orientation (2 points lost), attention/serial sevens (2 errors), copy of intersecting pentagons (incomplete), and the three-stage command (1 point). Clock drawing test shows all numbers present but bunched to the right side of the clock face, with hands set to an incorrect time. Unable to recall any of the 3 registered words after 5 minutes, even with phonemic cues. Naming intact for common objects but unable to name the stem of a watch or the eraser on a pencil. Repetition intact. Follows two-step commands but has difficulty with three-step commands. Judgment mildly impaired on hypothetical scenarios.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone in all extremities. No rigidity. Strength 5/5 throughout. No pronator drift. No tremor, chorea, or myoclonus.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick in all extremities. Vibration mildly diminished at bilateral great toes, otherwise intact. Proprioception intact at the toes bilaterally.
